"type_of_paper": "Observational + modeling study of a lunar occultation of a carbon-rich AGB star",
"executive_summary": "This paper presents high-speed, multi-wavelength observations of a lunar occultation of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (also known as OH 06.86-1.5 and IRAS 18036-2344), obtained on 28 Aug 2001 with the pMIRAS spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The observations span a continuous wavelength range of 1-4 microns, with a resolving power varying from about 20 at the short end to about 100 at the long end, and a time resolution of 8 msec that yields milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors compare these data with two calibration stars, IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2), which have no detectable circumstellar dust, to characterize the limitations of the observation and analysis process. The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. The authors therefore use the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell and fit both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yield a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K +/- 50 K, and an optical depth at 5 microns of 0.5 +/- 0.1. The observations are best fit by models with a density gradient of rho proportional to r^-2, or the gradient derived by Ivezi'c & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 x 10^-8 solar masses per year. However, the models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60-micron flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher mass-loss rate in the past. This work represents the first modeling of this star over the entire infrared wavelength region and separately resolves the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell.",

summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag
summary.field_subfield: Astrophysics: circumstellar mass loss and dust shells around AGB stars
summary.type_of_paper: Observational + modeling study of a lunar occultation of a carbon-rich AGB star
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents high-speed, multi-wavelength observations of a lunar occultation of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (also known as OH 06.86-1.5 and IRAS 18036-2344), obtained on 28 Aug 2001 with the pMIRAS spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The observations span a continuous wavelength range of 1-4 microns, with a resolving power varying from about 20 at the short end to about 100 at the long end, and a time resolution of 8 msec that yields milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors compare these data with two calibration stars, IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2), which have no detectable circumstellar dust, to characterize the limitations of the observation and analysis process. The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. The authors therefore use the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell and fit both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yield a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K +/- 50 K, and an optical depth at 5 microns of 0.5 +/- 0.1. The observations are best fit by models with a density gradient of rho proportional to r^-2, or the gradient derived by Ivezi'c & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 x 10^-8 solar masses per year. However, the models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60-micron flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher mass-loss rate in the past. This work represents the first modeling of this star over the entire infrared wavelength region and separately resolves the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell.

claims.description: The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model, indicating a circumstellar dust shell.
The dust temperature at the inner radius of the dust shell is Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K.
The radial density gradient of the best-fit models is close to r^-2, consistent with radiatively driven mass loss.
The IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents high-speed, multi-wavelength observations of a lunar occultation of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (also known as OH 06.86-1.5 and IRAS 18036-2344), obtained on 28 Aug 2001 with the pMIRAS spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The observations span a continuous wavelength range of 1-4 microns, with a resolving power varying from about 20 at the short end to about 100 at the long end, and a time resolution of 8 msec that yields milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors compare these data with two calibration stars, IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2), which have no detectable circumstellar dust, to characterize the limitations of the observation and analysis process. The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. The authors therefore use the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell and fit both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yield a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K +/- 50 K, and an optical depth at 5 microns of 0.5 +/- 0.1. The observations are best fit by models with a density gradient of rho proportional to r^-2, or the gradient derived by Ivezi'c & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 x 10^-8 solar masses per year. However, the models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60-micron flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher mass-loss rate in the past. This work represents the first modeling of this star over the entire infrared wavelength region and separately resolves the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars supplies much of the heavy elements and solid particles in the interstellar medium. The mechanisms of AGB mass loss are thought to involve radiation pressure and stellar pulsation, but details are poorly understood. Studies of circumstellar shell structure can clarify uncertainties about mass-loss processes. Molecular line and deep imaging studies have revealed periodic mass-loss variations producing 'rings' in radial distributions. Angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec are required to study the inner regions of circumstellar shells. Lunar occultation and multi-aperture interferometry have pushed resolutions to the milli-arcsecond level. Most interferometric observations have been made in only one or two broad bands, limiting spatial and spectral detail. AFGL 5440 is a carbon-rich AGB star with a well-characterized distance and photometry.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 can be fit by a single-size model or require a circumstellar shell. The authors hypothesize that the observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar dust shell from mass loss. They predict that a full radiative transfer model is needed to fit both the occultation fringes and the spectral energy distribution. They predict a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with Tmax around 950 K. They predict a density gradient close to r^-2 for a radiatively driven wind. They predict that the IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or a higher past mass-loss rate.

Methodological Details
The study observed a lunar occultation of the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440 (aka OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344). Observations were made during an immersion occultation event on 28 Aug 2001 at approximately 02:44:00 UT. The Moon elevation was 36 degrees, the Sun was 17 degrees below the horizon, and the lunar phase was 0.72. The position angle of the occultation on the lunar limb was 54 degrees. Observations were made with the pMIRAS instrument on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The instrument is a long/wide slit, high-speed spectrophotometer using a NaCl prism to disperse light onto a 32x100 pixel portion of a 256^2 InSb array. The slit width was set at about 5 arcsec for typical seeing of 1.5 arcsec. The detector is read-out every 8 msec, with photon integration over essentially the full 8 msec time. The observations cover the 1 - 4µm spectral region with resolving power varying from about 20 to about 100. The time resolution of 8 msec permits an effective angular resolution of a couple milli-arcsec. The plate scale in the spatial direction is 0.4 arcsec/pixel. The instrument is read-noise limited shortward of 2.5µm and background-limited longward of 3µm. A typical observation consists of taking 5000 frames centered on the occultation event. The buffer holds the most recent 5000 frames to accommodate errors in predicted occultation times of up to 10 seconds. The comparison stars IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2) were observed on 29 Jun 2001 and 26 Aug 2001. The data reduction uses a cross-correlation algorithm to shift images to the same wavelength/pixel scale. Sky subtraction uses sky measurements on either side of the stellar spectrum from the long slit. The end result is a sequence of about 100 light curves with a few hundred frames centered on the event. Wavelength calibration fits the NaCl dispersion function to the J, H, K, and L atmospheric transmission maxima. The wavelength calibration accuracy is probably good to ±0.01 lambda throughout the 1 - 4µm region. No flux calibration was attempted due to variable instrumental efficiency and non-photometric sky conditions. The stellar magnitudes in the literature are consistent with derived values within ±30%.

Procedures And Architectures
The fringe pattern is a convolution of blurring parameters including aperture, integration time, bandwidth, and source size/structure. The standard procedure is to model the blurring parameters with various source models to find the best fit. The basic fringe frequency (lunar shadow speed) must also be fit due to uncertainties in the lunar limb shape. The modeling began with a uniform disk as the simplest model for AFGL 5440, IRC+00233, and HD 155292. A simple chi-squared test is used for the best model, allowing one or more parameters to vary. For the comparison stars, a single source size was assumed for the entire wavelength range. The expected angular size of IRC+00233 is 3.5 mas, and HD 155292 is 0.6 mas, from blackbody and B-K color relations. The best fit size for IRC+00233 is between 4.5 and 5.0 mas. For HD 155292, all uniform-disk models with a size less than about 3 mas fit the data reasonably well. AFGL 5440 was fit with an example 11 mas uniform disk to demonstrate the poor fit. The DUSTY radiative transfer code (Ivezi'c, Nenkova & Elitzur 1999) was used to model the circumstellar shell. The approach was to choose input parameters and vary the dust optical depth to find the best fit to the energy distribution. The dust composition was assumed to be carbon-rich, typically a combination of amorphous carbon, silicon carbide, and graphite. The critical parameters are the dust temperature at the inner radius and the radial density gradient. The outer radius makes essentially no difference at wavelengths less than 60µm as long as it is at least 100 times the inner radius. More than 200 models were explored to understand the effect of varying input parameters. Two grain size distributions were tested: the MRN slope and the KMH shape.

Key Results
The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model. The dust temperature at the inner radius of the dust shell is Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K. Models with a maximum dust temperature below 900 K did not have enough hot dust to fit the occultation fringes at the longer wavelengths. The radial density gradient of models with a reasonable fit was close to r^-2. Models with a density gradient of r^-1.8 came closer to producing the IRAS 60µm flux but did not fit the 5 - 20µm energy distribution well. Models with a density gradient of r^-2.2 can fit the energy distribution out to 20µm but have worse fits to the IRAS 60µm flux. The optical depth for best fit at the fiducial wavelength of 5µm was typically in the range 0.3 - 0.6. The best-fit optical depth at 5µm is 0.5 ± 0.1. The best-fit dust composition included a small amount of SiC with comparable amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite. The physical inner radius of the dust shell is 3.7x10^14 cm, or an angular radius of 11 mas at 2.25 kpc. The angular diameter of the central star is of order 3 mas. The dust mass-loss rate implied by the derived optical depth and density dependence is 6.5 x 10^-8 solar masses per year. The best-fit model utilized roughly equal amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite in addition to a small amount of SiC. The dust emissivity is epsilon proportional to lambda^-1.3, consistent with amorphous carbon-rich dust. The IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit by any similar model without graphite. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC failed to fit the 60µm flux by factors of 3 or more. The gas mass-loss rate derived by Groenewegen et al. (2002) is 3.1x10^-5 solar masses per year. The gas-to-dust mass ratio implied by Groenewegen et al. (2002) is 600. The inner dust shell temperature is nearly a factor of two below the expected condensation temperatures.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observations separately resolve the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell. The dust density gradient is consistent with radiatively driven mass loss. The inner radius constraint follows from the fact that dust cooler than 900 K cannot emit sufficiently to produce the required 3 - 4µm emission. The inclusion of graphite was driven by its relatively flat emissivity between 10 and 50µm, enabling the fit to the IRAS 60µm flux. The failure to fit the 60µm flux may imply a recent decrease in mass-loss rate from the time when the far-IR-emitting dust was ejected. This result is contrary to the large amount of evidence against substantial amounts of graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The proposed higher past mass-loss rate is comparable to the period of fluctuation seen by Mauron & Huggins (2000) for IRC+10216. The dust mass-loss rate constrains the recent dust mass-loss rate for AFGL 5440.

Contradictions And Limitations
The models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60µm flux without graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. The inclusion of graphite is contrary to the large amount of evidence against substantial amounts of graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The discrepancy around 1.7µm for IRC+00233 has no good explanation and may be due to systematic noise or a real photospheric difference. The data are limited by spectral resolution and signal-to-noise ratio to accuracies on the order of ±2 mas. The wavelength calibration accuracy is probably good to ±0.01 lambda, but no flux calibration was attempted. The predicted times of occultation events are often in error by as much as 10 seconds. The lunar limb roughness can produce differences in the predicted shadow speed up to several tens of percent. The study did not attempt to extract details of the stellar photosphere or a thorough examination of all possible dust size/composition models. The study did not try to find any better than superficial agreement with the IRAS LRS data. The range of optical properties for different forms of amorphous carbon was not explored. The uncertainties in model assumptions and absolute dust opacities, particularly at longer infrared wavelengths, reinforce the overall uncertainties. The distance of 2.25 kpc is assumed, and the angular radius of 11 mas depends on this value.

Claims
The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model, indicating a circumstellar dust shell. A single source size was unlikely to fit over the entire 1 - 4µm bandwidth. The 11 mas uniform disk provides a passable fit in the mid-range but produces fringes that are too sharp at the longer wavelengths and too broadened at the shortest wavelengths. The observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar shell of material due to mass loss. The uniform disk model provides a very good fit to the observations for the comparison stars. The observations separately resolve the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell.
The dust temperature at the inner radius of the dust shell is Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K. The dust temperature at the inner radius of the dust shell was of order 950K ± 50K. Models with a maximum dust temperature below 900 K did not have enough hot dust to fit the occultation fringes at the longer wavelengths. The inner radius constraint follows from the fact that dust cooler than 900 K cannot emit sufficiently to produce the required 3 - 4µm emission. The inner dust shell temperature is nearly a factor of two below the expected condensation temperatures. Ivezi'c & Elitzur (1996) derived an inner dust shell temperature substantially lower than ours, about 750 K. The inner radius of the dust shell is physically 3.7x10^14 cm, or an angular radius of 11 mas at 2.25 kpc.
The radial density gradient of the best-fit models is close to r^-2, consistent with radiatively driven mass loss. The radial density gradient of models with a reasonable fit was close to r−2. The density gradient is consistent with that expected for radiatively driven mass loss. The gradient matches the Ivezi'c & Elitzur gradient for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. Models with a density gradient of r^-2.2 can fit the energy distribution out to 20µm but have worse fits to the IRAS 60µm flux. The observations constrain the dust density gradient in the innermost part of the circumstellar shell.
The IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. The IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit by any similar model without graphite. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC failed to fit the 60µm flux by factors of 3 or more. The factor that drove us to include graphite was its relatively flat emissivity between 10 and 50µm. The inclusion of graphite is contrary to the large amount of evidence against substantial amounts of graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The failure to fit the 60µm flux may imply a recent decrease in mass-loss rate from the time when the far-IR-emitting dust was ejected.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study explored more than 200 models to understand the effect of varying input parameters. Models with a maximum dust temperature below 900 K did not have enough hot dust to fit the occultation fringes at the longer wavelengths. Models with a density gradient of r^-1.8 came closer to producing the IRAS 60µm flux but did not fit the 5 - 20µm energy distribution well. Models with a density gradient of r^-2.2 can fit the energy distribution out to 20µm but have worse fits to the IRAS 60µm flux. The outer radius makes essentially no difference at wavelengths less than 60µm as long as it is at least 100 times the inner radius. We found that we could obtain reasonably good fits with either the MRN or KMH grain size distributions. The other carbon-rich compositions produced reasonable fits except at the longest wavelengths or in the 11µm SiC feature.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first modeling of AFGL 5440 over the entire infrared wavelength region, separately resolving the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell. 2. The strongest evidence is the constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K and optical depth at 5µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. 3. The future path is to resolve the discrepancy in the IRAS 60µm flux, which may require graphite or a recent decrease in mass-loss rate.
